title: Stream-Fusion Scheduling — Fairness Rationale & Sketch
body:
Purpose
This note captures a compact, opinionated sketch for a streaming-first scheduling approach ("Stream-Fusion") aimed at reconciling token-level responsiveness with request-level fairness in the Redwood serving runtime. The goal is to surface practical tradeoffs, a lightweight algorithm sketch, kernel/kv-cache interactions, and an experiment plan.

Context and motivation
We need a scheduler that: (1) gives low latency for interactive requests (short outputs, chat), (2) maintains high throughput for bulk generation, (3) prevents starvation of high-priority or long-running requests, and (4) cooperates with the kernel selection and KV cache to avoid excessive context thrash. Existing sketches either prioritize tokens (maximizing packing/throughput) or requests (preserving request-closure semantics). Stream-Fusion tries to operate in-between: treat the scheduler as a streaming conductor that blends token streaming windows with per-request credit accounting.

Key ideas (high level)
- Streaming windows: runtime exposes short micro-windows (configurable in ms or token budget) during which any ready request can contribute tokens. These windows are the unit for kernel selection and launch.
- Request credit: each request maintains a fairness credit that accrues based on waiting time and SLA tier. Credits are consumed when a request participates in a micro-window.
- Adaptive packing preference: within a window, prefer grouping tokens from requests that improve kernel utilization (same seq length bucket, same model variant, same quantization) but only if their effective credit share exceeds a threshold.
- KV-aware locality bonus: requests whose KV cache entries are warm on a worker get a scheduling bonus to reduce KV invalidation and kernel warmup.

Why this differs from pure token-level vs. request-level approaches
- Pure token-level: maximizes GPU occupancy by filling every slot with any token, but it can cause frequent preemption of long-running requests and unpredictable per-request latency tails.
- Pure request-level: schedules whole requests or contiguous token blocks, which simplifies fairness but underutilizes parallelism when requests have heterogenous decoding speed/lengths.
- Stream-Fusion: trades small, bounded context switches (micro-windows) for better packing while keeping per-request fairness guarantees via credit accounting.

Fairness model and metrics
We propose a two-dimensional fairness model:
- Progress fairness (PF): fraction of required tokens produced per request normalized by SLA-weighted demand over time window T. PF ~ 1 for ideal fairness.
- Tail latency fairness (TLF): focus on 95/99th-percentile completion latency for different request classes.
- Starvation bound (SB): maximum time a request with at least min_credit can be delayed without progress. SB is configurable and must be enforced.

Credit rules (sketch)
- Initial credit: requests start with base_credit proportional to priority_tier (e.g., free=1, paid=3, enterprise=10).
- Accrual: credit += accrual_rate * waiting_seconds. accrual_rate tunable per tier.
- Spend: when a request contributes k tokens in a micro-window, credit -= k * cost_per_token. cost_per_token normalizes different decoding costs (e.g., sampling cheap vs. expensive sampling).
- Negative credit allowed up to a bounded overdraft; beyond that request is deprioritized until replenished.

Micro-window orchestration
- Window duration: dynamic between 4ms and 40ms (heuristic). Short windows favor latency; longer windows favor throughput. Window length adapts to observed token arrival rates and tail SLOs.
- Window admission: at window start the scheduler forms a candidate set of requests in READY state. It computes effective_score = credit * locality_bonus * kernel_affinity. Requests are admitted into the window by descending effective_score until GPU slots filled or min_batch_unit reached.

Kernel selection and sequence-length bucketing
- Kernel choice depends on the dominant sequence length in the assembled batch and quantization profile. To avoid degenerative kernels, the scheduler will prefer batches with sequence-length variance below a threshold; if variance high, schedule sub-batches with lower variance.
- Kernel affinity: requests previously executed on a worker that retains a compatible kernel get an affinity bonus. This reduces kernel churn.

KV cache & eviction interactions
- KV locality bonus increases effective_score if the selected worker already holds a warm KV for the request’s context.
- To avoid excessive memory pressure, the scheduler tracks estimated KV footprint per request and penalizes admission when worker memory budget would be exceeded.
- Eviction-aware batching: if admitting a new request triggers eviction of a hot KV, compute projected cost (eviction_cost = cold_start_tokens * token_cost) and subtract from effective_score.

Pseudocode sketch
1) On window_tick():
   ready = pop_ready_requests(timeout_cutoff)
   compute credit for each r in ready (apply accrual)
   for r in ready: compute locality_bonus(r), kernel_affinity(r)
   sort ready by effective_score = credit * locality_bonus * kernel_affinity
   batch = []
   while gpu_slots_remaining and ready not empty:
       cand = ready.pop(0)
       if batch_accepts(cand): batch.append(cand)
       else: deferred.append(cand)
   launch_kernel_for(batch)
   for r in batch: r.credit -= r.allocated_tokens * cost_per_token

Notes on batch_accepts(cand): checks sequence-length variance, estimated KV memory, and minimal per-request token chunk (e.g., min 1 token; can be raised for long requests).

Preemption and re-entrancy
- Micro-windows permit re-entrancy: a long-running request will appear across multiple windows. Preemption happens only at window boundary, limiting context thrash.
- If a high-priority request arrives mid-window and immediate latency is required, scheduler can trigger an emergency window flush (subject to rate limits) to accommodate it.

Example scenarios
- Many short chat messages: short windows, high accrual for new requests, strong locality bonus keeps KV reuse high. Scheduler packs many 1–4 token contributions and keeps latency low.
- Mixed short + long: credit accrual ensures short requests eventually get slots; long requests get small guaranteed allocations each window to make progress (prevent starvation).
- Bulk generation burst: windows lengthen, packing favors throughput, kernel affinity steering reduces kernel churn.

Experiment plan (concrete)
1) Offline sim: replay production traces (1 week) with a configurable Stream-Fusion sim. Metrics: GPU utilization, PF, TLF, SB. 2) A/B small fleet: enable Stream-Fusion opt-in for 10% traffic with telemetry. Compare to baseline continuous token-level scheduler. 3) Kernel churn measurement: instrument kernel load/unload counts per minute. 4) KV impact: measure cache hit rate, eviction count, estimated extra decode tokens due to cold starts.

Open questions and risks
- Tuning complexity: multiple knobs (window duration, accrual rates, locality bonus) may interact in surprising ways. Mitigation: default sensible presets and automated tuning based on SLO violations.
- Implementation cost: need lightweight per-request state and fast scoring at window boundaries. Aim for O(n log n) with small constants; consider shard-local schedulers to reduce coordination.
- Billing/observability: partial-token scheduling complicates per-request accounting; ensure cost attribution maps to actual tokens produced.

Immediate action items
- Prototype sim (owner: Maya) using last-quarter traces. Target: lightweight Rust sim that mirrors current token-level scheduler inputs. (ETA 3 weeks)
- Spike kernel-affinity estimator (owner: Liam) to quantify kernel churn benefit of affinity bonus. (ETA 2 weeks)
- Add KV footprint metadata to request lifecycle (owner: Sofia) to enable eviction-aware scoring. (ETA 2 weeks)

Appendix: short glossary
- micro-window: short scheduling epoch (ms) used to assemble token groups.
- credit: abstract fairness currency per request.
- locality_bonus: multiplier if KV/cache/kernel warm on a worker.
- kernel_affinity: heuristic estimating lower setup cost when grouping requests.

References
- internal PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/842
- related ticket: JIRA SR-319


This is intentionally concise; next iteration will include a lightweight simulation snapshot, perf targets for PF and TLF, and JSON logs schema for telemetry.
